Topics.Title: Transaction Fundamentals
Topics.Summary: Introduces what a database transaction is, why grouping operations into a single logical unit protects data integrity, and the BEGIN–EXECUTE–COMMIT/ROLLBACK lifecycle. Uses the classic bank transfer scenario to show the danger of unprotected multi-step operations.

Elements.Title: What Is a Transaction?
Elements.BodyText: A transaction is a logical unit of work containing one or more database operations that are treated as a single, indivisible action. It either completes entirely or has no effect at all.
Elements.Notes: Think of a transaction as a wrapper placed around several SQL statements so the database treats them as one action.

Items.Text: All operations within a transaction succeed together or fail together as a single unit.
The database moves from one valid, consistent state to another valid state.
Concurrent transactions execute in isolation so they do not interfere with one another.
Once committed, the changes are permanent and survive system failures.
A transaction may contain INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT statements across multiple tables.

Elements.Title: Why Transactions Matter: The Bank Transfer Problem
Elements.BodyText: The classic bank transfer illustrates the danger of running multi-step operations without transaction protection. Money must never be created or destroyed by a partial update.
Elements.Notes: Without a transaction: UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE AccountID = 1; -- crash here -- UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE AccountID = 2;

Items.Text: A transfer requires two updates: debit the source account and credit the destination account.
If the system crashes between the two statements, the debited money simply disappears.
Wrapping both updates in BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT TRANSACTION guarantees both apply or neither does.
The same risk applies to inventory deductions, seat bookings, and any multi-step business operation.
Transactions remove the need for applications to write complex manual clean-up logic after failures.

Elements.Title: The Transaction Lifecycle
Elements.BodyText: Every explicit transaction follows a predictable lifecycle of four stages that the developer controls. Understanding these stages is the foundation of all transaction programming.
Elements.Notes: A transaction must always end in either a COMMIT or a ROLLBACK — never be left open.

Items.Text: BEGIN: the transaction starts and the database begins tracking changes in the transaction log.
EXECUTE: one or more database operations are performed, with changes held pending.
COMMIT: on success, all changes are made permanent and visible to other sessions.
ROLLBACK: on failure, every change made since BEGIN is undone and the database returns to its prior state.
Locks acquired during the transaction are released when the transaction ends.

Elements.Title: When to Use an Explicit Transaction
Elements.BodyText: Not every statement needs an explicit transaction, so it helps to know which scenarios demand one. The deciding factor is whether multiple related changes must stand or fall together.
Elements.Notes: Single-statement work is already atomic under autocommit mode, so wrapping it adds overhead without benefit.

Items.Text: Use an explicit transaction whenever two or more related operations must succeed or fail as a unit.
A single INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE can rely on autocommit — no explicit transaction is needed.
Financial operations such as transfers and payments always warrant explicit transactions with full validation.
Order processing that touches Orders, OrderItems and Inventory is a textbook multi-step case.
User registration that creates an account, profile, preferences and role records also belongs in one transaction.

Elements.Title: A Complete Transaction Example
Elements.BodyText: Combining multiple operations into one transaction makes the all-or-nothing guarantee concrete. The order and inventory example shows three dependent statements protected as one unit.
Elements.Notes: BEGIN TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO Orders ...; INSERT INTO OrderItems ...; UPDATE Inventory SET Quantity = Quantity - 2 ...; COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Items.Text: The order header is inserted first and its generated key is captured with SCOPE_IDENTITY().
The related order line items are inserted using that key.
Inventory quantities are reduced to reflect the goods sold.
If any single step fails, none of the three changes are retained in the database.
Without the transaction, an order could exist with no items or inventory could drop with no matching order.

Elements.Title: Transactions and Critical Business Data
Elements.BodyText: Transactions are most essential where incorrect or partial data carries real business consequences. They are a core tool for maintaining data integrity in multi-step operations.
Elements.Notes: Data integrity, business criticality, simplified development and system reliability are the four main reasons transactions matter.

Items.Text: Money, inventory, and other critical business data demand transactional protection.
Transactions prevent corruption and inconsistencies that arise from partial updates or concurrent access.
Developers can rely on the database's guarantees instead of hand-coding recovery logic.
Industries such as finance, healthcare, e-commerce and airline reservations depend on these guarantees.
Transactions also improve overall system reliability by making the database resilient to unexpected failures.

Topics.Title: The ACID Properties
Topics.Summary: Explains Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability with definitions, analogies, SQL examples, and the implementation mechanisms (logging, constraints, locking, WAL) behind each. Also examines the benefits, costs, and trade-offs of relaxing each property.

Elements.Title: ACID Overview: Four Guarantees of Reliable Transactions
Elements.BodyText: ACID is an acronym describing the four fundamental properties that guarantee reliable transaction processing in a database system. Together they protect data integrity during concurrent access and system failures.
Elements.Notes: ACID is a set of rules, not an algorithm — each database vendor must choose algorithms (logging, locking, versioning) to implement them.

Items.Text: A stands for Atomicity, C for Consistency, I for Isolation, and D for Durability.
ACID guarantees matter most in financial, e-commerce, healthcare, and other business-critical systems.
They simplify development because programmers can rely on the engine instead of hand-coding error recovery and concurrency control.
Full ACID compliance carries performance costs, so engines expose tuning options such as isolation levels.

Elements.Title: Atomicity: All or Nothing
Elements.BodyText: Atomicity means every operation in a transaction succeeds or they all fail; there is no partial completion. Like an atom, the transaction cannot be split into smaller independently-surviving parts.
Elements.Notes: Example: BEGIN TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO Orders...; INSERT INTO OrderItems...; UPDATE Inventory SET Quantity = Quantity - 2...; COMMIT TRANSACTION; — all three statements complete or none do.

Items.Text: A bank transfer must debit the source account and credit the destination account together, or neither.
Implementation relies on a transaction log that records every change made inside the transaction.
If the transaction fails or the server crashes, ROLLBACK uses the log to undo incomplete work and restore the prior state.
SQL Server uses write-ahead logging in .ldf files, MySQL InnoDB uses redo logs, and Oracle combines redo logs with undo tablespaces.
Atomicity is fundamental and cannot be relaxed; its only cost is transaction log overhead.

Elements.Title: Consistency: Valid State to Valid State
Elements.BodyText: Consistency guarantees that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving all constraints and business rules. Think of a balanced scale that stays balanced before and after the operation.
Elements.Notes: Example: UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 1000 WHERE AccountID = 1; — if a CHECK constraint forbids negative balances, the violation forces a rollback and no negative balance is ever stored.

Items.Text: Enforcement comes from CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints, plus triggers and application-level business logic.
The engine validates changes before allowing a COMMIT; a constraint violation aborts the transaction.
PostgreSQL adds DEFERRABLE constraints so checking can be postponed until commit time.
The benefit is enforced data integrity; the cost is constraint-checking overhead on every write.
Relaxing consistency is dangerous and not recommended, because it allows corrupt or invalid data to persist.

Elements.Title: Isolation: Concurrent Transactions Don't Collide
Elements.BodyText: Isolation ensures concurrent transactions execute independently without interfering with each other's intermediate results. It works like separate lanes on a highway that keep traffic from colliding.
Elements.Notes: Example: a transaction that runs UPDATE Products SET Price = 100 keeps that price invisible to others until COMMIT. Classic scenario: two users booking the last seat on a flight — only one booking can succeed.

Items.Text: Implementation uses locking (shared, exclusive, update locks) and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC).
MVCC lets each transaction read a consistent snapshot of row versions as of its start time, reducing blocking.
Optimistic concurrency control allows work to proceed without locks and checks for conflicts at commit.
SQL defines isolation levels — READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE — plus SNAPSHOT in SQL Server.
Isolation is the one property safely tuned: lowering the level increases concurrency but permits anomalies such as dirty or phantom reads.

Elements.Title: Durability: Committed Means Permanent
Elements.BodyText: Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes, power loss, and restarts. It is like writing in permanent marker rather than pencil.
Elements.Notes: Example: after COMMIT on an INSERT INTO Orders, the order remains saved even if the server crashes immediately afterward, because the log replays the change on restart.

Items.Text: Write-ahead logging (WAL) writes log records to disk before the data pages are updated.
Recovery on restart replays committed log records and undoes uncommitted ones.
PostgreSQL uses WAL plus fsync controlled by synchronous_commit; MySQL InnoDB uses a doublewrite buffer and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit.
Replication and regular backups extend durability by protecting against whole-server loss.
The cost is disk I/O and slower commits; durability should only be relaxed in specific, well-understood scenarios.

Elements.Title: ACID Trade-offs and When to Relax
Elements.BodyText: Each ACID property delivers a benefit at a measurable cost, and the properties differ in whether they can safely be weakened. Understanding the trade-offs guides configuration decisions.
Elements.Notes: Distributed systems complicate matters: the CAP theorem forces a choice among consistency, availability and partition tolerance, which is why AP stores like Cassandra offer only eventual consistency.

Items.Text: Atomicity: benefit is the all-or-nothing guarantee, cost is log overhead, and it cannot be relaxed.
Consistency: benefit is enforced integrity, cost is constraint checking, and relaxing it is dangerous.
Isolation: benefit is non-interference, cost is locking, blocking and reduced concurrency, and it can be tuned through isolation levels.
Durability: benefit is crash survival, cost is disk I/O and slower commits, and it should be relaxed only in special cases such as in-memory caching.
Traditional RDBMSs like SQL Server, PostgreSQL and Oracle give the strongest ACID guarantees for critical applications.

Topics.Title: ACID Implementation Across Database Platforms
Topics.Summary: Compares how SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB, Oracle, and major NoSQL systems implement each ACID property. Connects these differences to the CAP theorem and the consistency/availability choices made by distributed data stores.

Elements.Title: ACID Is a Standard, Not an Algorithm
Elements.BodyText: ACID defines four guarantees that every database must provide, but each vendor chooses its own internal algorithms to deliver them. Understanding the shared building blocks makes platform comparisons much easier.
Elements.Notes: This is why research into a specific product is required: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL all satisfy ACID yet use different log structures, file names and configuration switches.

Items.Text: Atomicity is almost always delivered through write-ahead or redo logging plus rollback/undo capability.
Consistency is enforced by constraints (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE), triggers and data validation performed before commit.
Isolation is achieved through locking, multi-version concurrency control (MVCC), or optimistic concurrency checks at commit time.
Durability relies on flushing log records to disk before commit, supplemented by replication, backups and recovery replay.
The underlying principles are identical across systems; only the implementation details and tuning knobs differ.

Elements.Title: SQL Server and PostgreSQL Implementations
Elements.BodyText: Both SQL Server and PostgreSQL are considered to offer very strong ACID guarantees, but they emphasise different concurrency mechanisms.
Elements.Notes: PostgreSQL's MVCC is often cited for excellent concurrency because readers never block writers; SQL Server achieves similar behaviour only when snapshot isolation or read-committed snapshot is enabled.

Items.Text: SQL Server uses Write-Ahead Logging stored in .ldf transaction log files for atomicity and durability, with checkpoints and full, bulk-logged or simple recovery models.
SQL Server enforces consistency with CHECK, FOREIGN KEY and UNIQUE constraints plus triggers and rules.
SQL Server isolation combines locking with row versioning and offers five isolation levels including SNAPSHOT.
PostgreSQL writes its WAL into the pg_wal directory and controls durability through WAL plus fsync and the synchronous_commit setting.
PostgreSQL supports DEFERRABLE constraints and relies on MVCC with four isolation levels for high concurrency.

Elements.Title: MySQL (InnoDB) and Oracle Implementations
Elements.BodyText: MySQL's InnoDB engine and Oracle Database both use redo logging, but Oracle adds undo structures that also power read consistency.
Elements.Notes: InnoDB's innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit setting is a classic example of trading durability for speed; Oracle's COMMIT NOWAIT option offers a similar trade-off.

Items.Text: InnoDB provides atomicity through redo logs (ib_logfile0, ib_logfile1) and durability via the doublewrite buffer plus redo logs.
InnoDB supports foreign key constraints, though constraint support was more limited in older MySQL versions and storage engines.
InnoDB isolation mixes MVCC with locking across four isolation levels.
Oracle uses online redo logs together with undo tablespaces to support both rollback and read consistency.
Oracle isolation is MVCC-based using undo segments, defaulting to READ COMMITTED with SERIALIZABLE available.

Elements.Title: ACID Support in NoSQL Databases
Elements.BodyText: NoSQL systems have moved toward ACID support, but usually with scope limits and performance trade-offs that differ sharply from relational engines.
Elements.Notes: The common pattern is strong guarantees at the single-document or single-item level, with multi-record transactions available but constrained.

Items.Text: MongoDB offers full ACID for single documents and, since version 4.0, multi-document transactions, at a performance cost on distributed operations.
Cassandra provides only limited guarantees, relying on eventual consistency with lightweight transactions for special cases.
Redis gives ACID behaviour for single commands and supports multi-command transactions, but durability is optional because it is in-memory.
DynamoDB supports ACID for a single item and TransactWriteItems for multi-item work, limited to 25 items per transaction.
Choosing a NoSQL store means explicitly accepting these scope and consistency limits.

Elements.Title: The CAP Theorem and Distributed Trade-offs
Elements.BodyText: In distributed systems the CAP theorem states that only two of Consistency, Availability and Partition Tolerance can be guaranteed simultaneously. This constraint explains why distributed stores relax ACID.
Elements.Notes: Partition tolerance is effectively mandatory in any real network, so the practical decision is between consistency (CP) and availability (AP).

Items.Text: Consistency means every node sees the same data at the same time.
Availability means the system keeps responding to requests even when some nodes are unhealthy.
Partition tolerance means the system continues operating despite network failures between nodes.
Traditional RDBMS are described as CA systems and deliver full ACID.
MongoDB and HBase lean CP, preserving strong ACID semantics at the expense of availability during partitions.
Cassandra and DynamoDB lean AP, favouring availability with eventual consistency and limited ACID.

Elements.Title: Choosing a Platform Based on ACID Requirements
Elements.BodyText: Matching the database engine to the integrity requirements of the workload is a core design decision. The strength of ACID guarantees should follow the business risk of incorrect data.
Elements.Notes: Relational engines such as SQL Server, PostgreSQL and Oracle remain the default for financial, medical and other critical applications where data integrity is paramount.

Items.Text: Use a full-ACID relational engine for money movement, healthcare records, reservations and other high-integrity workloads.
Consider AP NoSQL stores for high-volume, high-availability workloads where eventual consistency is acceptable.
Remember that relaxing isolation is a supported tuning option, while relaxing atomicity or consistency is not advisable.
Check platform-specific durability settings, because some engines allow commits to return before the log is flushed.
When comparing products, evaluate each ACID property separately rather than accepting a blanket 'ACID compliant' claim.

Topics.Title: T-SQL Transaction Control
Topics.Summary: Covers explicit, implicit, and autocommit transaction modes along with BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVE TRANSACTION statements. Includes savepoints for partial rollback and techniques for inspecting transaction state with @@TRANCOUNT and DMVs.

Elements.Title: Transaction Modes in SQL Server
Elements.BodyText: SQL Server runs every statement inside some kind of transaction, and the mode determines when a transaction starts and ends. T-SQL supports autocommit, explicit, and implicit transaction modes.
Elements.Notes: Autocommit is the default mode; most applications only switch to explicit transactions when multiple statements must succeed or fail together.

Items.Text: Autocommit mode treats each individual statement as its own transaction that commits automatically on success.
Explicit mode begins when you issue BEGIN TRANSACTION and ends only at COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
Implicit mode is enabled with SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS ON, which auto-starts a transaction but still requires an explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
Turn implicit mode off with SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS OFF to return to autocommit behaviour.
Use autocommit for a single INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and explicit transactions for multi-step operations.

Elements.Title: Explicit Transactions with BEGIN and COMMIT
Elements.BodyText: Explicit transactions group several related statements into one atomic unit of work. They are the standard approach for multi-step business operations such as price updates with history logging.
Elements.Notes: Example: BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE Products SET Price = Price * 1.1 WHERE CategoryID = 1; INSERT INTO PriceHistory ...; COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Items.Text: BEGIN TRANSACTION (or BEGIN TRAN) marks the start of the unit of work.
COMMIT TRANSACTION (or COMMIT) makes all changes within the transaction permanent.
The lifecycle is BEGIN → EXECUTE operations → COMMIT on success or ROLLBACK on failure.
Wrap the body in BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH so failures can be rolled back and re-thrown.
Validate inputs before BEGIN TRANSACTION to keep the transaction short and reduce lock contention.

Elements.Title: ROLLBACK and Undoing Work
Elements.BodyText: ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the transaction began, restoring the database to its prior valid state. It is the safety net that enforces atomicity.
Elements.Notes: The classic bank transfer illustrates the risk: without a transaction, a crash between the debit and the credit makes money disappear.

Items.Text: ROLLBACK TRANSACTION (or ROLLBACK) reverses all uncommitted changes in the current transaction.
A ROLLBACK issued at any nesting level rolls back the entire outermost transaction.
Place ROLLBACK inside a CATCH block, followed by THROW to propagate the original error.
SET XACT_ABORT ON causes SQL Server to roll back automatically when any run-time error occurs.
Never leave a transaction open after an error — always commit or roll back.

Elements.Title: Savepoints and Partial Rollback
Elements.BodyText: SAVE TRANSACTION creates a named savepoint inside an active transaction so that only part of the work can be undone. This allows recovery from a failed step without discarding everything already done.
Elements.Notes: Example: SAVE TRANSACTION AfterOrderInsert; ... ROLLBACK TRANSACTION AfterOrderInsert; — the order header insert survives while the failed item insert is discarded.

Items.Text: Syntax is SAVE TRANSACTION SavePointName, placed before a risky operation.
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION SavePointName undoes only the work performed after that savepoint.
The outer transaction remains active and must still be committed or rolled back.
Savepoints enable alternative actions, such as logging the error and marking a record as 'Pending Review'.
Savepoints are preferable to nested BEGIN TRANSACTION when you need partial rollback behaviour.

Elements.Title: Inspecting Transaction State with @@TRANCOUNT
Elements.BodyText: @@TRANCOUNT reports the current transaction nesting depth for the session and is the key to safe transaction control. Checking it prevents errors from rolling back when no transaction exists.
Elements.Notes: Common pattern: IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

Items.Text: @@TRANCOUNT returns 0 when no transaction is active and a value greater than 0 for nesting depth.
Each BEGIN TRANSACTION increments @@TRANCOUNT; each COMMIT decrements it.
Always test @@TRANCOUNT before issuing ROLLBACK, especially inside CATCH blocks.
Use a flag variable so a nested procedure only commits the transaction it actually started.
Never assume the calling code has already opened a transaction.

Elements.Title: Monitoring Transactions with DMVs
Elements.BodyText: Dynamic management views and DBCC commands let you see which transactions are active, how long they have run, and what isolation settings are in effect.
Elements.Notes: Long-running transactions (over 10 seconds) signal high blocking and deadlock risk and should be investigated or redesigned.

Items.Text: sys.dm_tran_active_transactions lists all currently active transactions on the instance.
sys.dm_tran_session_transactions maps transactions to the sessions that own them.
Join these DMVs with sys.dm_exec_sessions and use transaction_begin_time to find long-running transactions.
DBCC USEROPTIONS displays the current session's transaction isolation level.
DBCC SQLPERF(LOGSPACE) reports transaction log usage across databases.

Topics.Title: Isolation Levels, Locking, and Concurrency
Topics.Summary: Compares READ UNCOMMITTED through SERIALIZABLE and SNAPSHOT isolation in terms of dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads versus concurrency. Examines SQL Server lock types, granularity, compatibility, lock hints, and strategies for detecting and preventing deadlocks.

Elements.Title: Concurrency Anomalies: Dirty, Non-Repeatable, and Phantom Reads
Elements.BodyText: Isolation levels exist to control three classic read anomalies that occur when transactions run concurrently. Understanding each anomaly is the key to choosing the right level.
Elements.Notes: Example: a REPEATABLE READ transaction locks the rows it read, but another session can still INSERT a new row matching the same WHERE clause, producing a phantom on the second read.

Items.Text: A dirty read occurs when a transaction reads data another transaction has changed but not yet committed, so the value may later be rolled back.
A non-repeatable read occurs when the same row is read twice in one transaction and returns different values because another transaction committed an update in between.
A phantom read occurs when a repeated range query returns additional rows because another transaction inserted data matching the predicate.
Higher isolation prevents more anomalies but places more locks and reduces concurrency.
The trade-off table maps each level to which anomalies it allows and its relative concurrency rating.

Elements.Title: READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED
Elements.BodyText: These are the two lowest isolation levels, trading consistency guarantees for throughput. READ COMMITTED is SQL Server's default.
Elements.Notes: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED; is useful for approximate reporting totals such as SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(TotalAmount) FROM Orders.

Items.Text: READ UNCOMMITTED (Level 0) places no shared locks, allows dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads, and gives maximum concurrency with no blocking.
Use READ UNCOMMITTED only for reporting queries where approximate data is acceptable and accuracy is not critical.
READ COMMITTED (Level 1) reads only committed data, preventing dirty reads while still allowing non-repeatable and phantom reads.
Within a READ COMMITTED transaction, a balance read as 1000 can return 1500 on a second read if another session commits an update.
READ COMMITTED is recommended for most applications as a balance of consistency and concurrency.

Elements.Title: REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE, and SNAPSHOT
Elements.BodyText: The higher isolation levels add protection against changing data during a transaction, with SNAPSHOT achieving consistency through row versioning instead of blocking.
Elements.Notes: SNAPSHOT requires ALTER DATABASE MyDatabase SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON; before SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT can be used.

Items.Text: REPEATABLE READ (Level 2) locks rows that are read so repeated reads return the same values, but new rows can still appear as phantoms.
SERIALIZABLE (Level 3) uses range locks to prevent inserts, updates, and deletes in the queried range, eliminating all anomalies at the cost of heavy blocking and deadlock risk.
SNAPSHOT isolation uses row versioning (MVCC) so each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data as of its start time.
With SNAPSHOT, readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, giving the highest concurrency of the consistent levels.
SNAPSHOT costs tempdb overhead to store row versions and can produce update conflicts that must be handled.

Elements.Title: Setting Isolation Levels in T-SQL
Elements.BodyText: Isolation can be specified at the session, transaction, or individual query level, and the current setting can be inspected at runtime.
Elements.Notes: Recommendation: use READ COMMITTED for most applications, consider SNAPSHOT for high-concurrency read-heavy workloads, and avoid READ UNCOMMITTED unless accuracy is unimportant.

Items.Text: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL <level>; applies to the session until changed or the connection ends.
Setting the level inside BEGIN TRANSACTION scopes the behaviour to that unit of work and is the recommended practice.
Query-level table hints such as WITH (READUNCOMMITTED) or WITH (NOLOCK) override the session setting for a single table reference.
DBCC USEROPTIONS reports the current transaction isolation level for the session.
sys.dm_tran_active_transactions and sys.dm_tran_session_transactions expose active transaction information.

Elements.Title: SQL Server Lock Types and Granularity
Elements.BodyText: SQL Server enforces isolation with locks that vary by mode and by the size of the resource they protect. Choosing granularity balances concurrency against memory overhead.
Elements.Notes: Intent locks (IS, IX, IU) are applied automatically to indicate the lock hierarchy, and schema locks (Sch-S, Sch-M) protect against DDL changes during queries.

Items.Text: Shared (S) locks are taken for SELECT statements and allow multiple concurrent readers.
Exclusive (X) locks are taken for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE and block all other lock requests.
Update (U) locks signal intent to update and help prevent conversion deadlocks during UPDATE operations.
Granularity ranges from row (RID) and key through page, extent, table, and database.
Finer granularity such as row locking maximizes concurrency but consumes more lock memory; coarser table locks use minimal memory but serialize access.

Elements.Title: Lock Compatibility, Hints, and Monitoring
Elements.BodyText: Whether a requested lock is granted depends on the compatibility matrix with existing locks; hints let developers override default behaviour, and DMVs expose current blocking.
Elements.Notes: Example hints: WITH (NOLOCK), WITH (HOLDLOCK), WITH (UPDLOCK), WITH (XLOCK), WITH (TABLOCK), WITH (ROWLOCK). Banking procedures often use WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) when reading a balance that will be updated.

Items.Text: Shared locks are compatible with other shared and update locks, but exclusive locks are incompatible with everything.
An update lock is compatible with existing shared locks but blocks other update and exclusive requests.
NOLOCK mimics READ UNCOMMITTED, HOLDLOCK holds locks until the transaction ends, and UPDLOCK/XLOCK escalate the lock mode taken by a read.
sys.dm_tran_locks shows resource type, request mode, and request status for the current session's locks.
Joining sys.dm_exec_requests to itself on blocking_session_id identifies blocker and blocked sessions and wait times; KILL terminates a blocking session but should be used with caution.

Elements.Title: Deadlocks: Detection, Handling, and Prevention
Elements.BodyText: A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, forcing SQL Server to choose a victim and roll it back. Most deadlocks are preventable through design.
Elements.Notes: Error number 1205 identifies a deadlock victim and is a good candidate for retry logic inside a CATCH block. DBCC TRACEON(1222, -1) logs deadlock details to the error log, and the system_health extended events ring buffer stores deadlock graphs.

Items.Text: A classic deadlock arises when Transaction 1 updates Account 1 then Account 2, while Transaction 2 updates Account 2 then Account 1.
Access tables and rows in a consistent order across all transactions, and keep transactions short and fast.
Use the lowest appropriate isolation level, consider SNAPSHOT isolation, and create indexes that avoid broad scan locks.
ROWLOCK hints can reduce lock escalation that contributes to deadlocks.
Detect deadlocks with trace flag 1222 or the system_health session and implement retry logic for the deadlock victim.

Topics.Title: Transactions in Stored Procedures and Error Handling
Topics.Summary: Shows proven patterns for encapsulating transactional logic in stored procedures using validation-first design, TRY...CATCH, XACT_ABORT, THROW, and error logging. Explains how SQL Server treats nested transactions and how to safely coordinate procedures with @@TRANCOUNT checks and savepoints.

Elements.Title: Encapsulating Transactions in Stored Procedures
Elements.BodyText: Stored procedures are the preferred place to put transactional logic because they centralize business rules, guarantee consistent error handling, and keep the unit of work on the server.
Elements.Notes: Example: usp_TransferFunds debits one account, credits another, writes a TransactionLog row, then commits — all inside one procedure.

Items.Text: Begin every procedure with SET NOCOUNT ON to suppress extra row-count messages.
Wrap the BEGIN TRANSACTION / COMMIT TRANSACTION block inside BEGIN TRY ... END TRY.
Return 0 on success and let the CATCH block signal failure to the caller.
Use OUTPUT parameters (such as @OrderID) to pass generated keys back to the caller.
Document the procedure's transaction expectations in the header so callers know whether it opens its own transaction.

Elements.Title: Validation-First Design
Elements.BodyText: All validation that can be done without locks should happen before BEGIN TRANSACTION so the transaction stays as short as possible and locks are held for a minimal time.
Elements.Notes: usp_CreateOrderWithValidation checks customer existence, product existence, and a positive quantity with RAISERROR and RETURN -1 before any transaction is opened.

Items.Text: Check referential existence with IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...) before opening the transaction.
Validate parameter ranges, such as rejecting quantities less than or equal to zero.
Raise an error and RETURN a negative code so the caller can distinguish validation failures.
Only checks that require locking (such as stock availability with UPDLOCK) belong inside the transaction.
Skipping validation to save time is listed explicitly as an anti-pattern.

Elements.Title: TRY...CATCH and @@TRANCOUNT Rollback Pattern
Elements.BodyText: The standard SQL Server pattern places the transaction inside TRY and the rollback inside CATCH, always guarded by a check on @@TRANCOUNT.
Elements.Notes: Critical rule: never let a transaction remain open after an error — every path must either commit or roll back.

Items.Text: Always test IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 before issuing ROLLBACK TRANSACTION to avoid an error when no transaction is active.
@@TRANCOUNT returns 0 when no transaction is open and a value greater than 0 for nesting depth.
Capture diagnostics with ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_SEVERITY(), ERROR_STATE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), and ERROR_LINE().
THROW (SQL Server 2012+) re-throws the original error with all details intact and is preferred over re-raising with RAISERROR.
RAISERROR(@ErrorMsg, 16, 1) is still used when you need to substitute a friendlier message.

Elements.Title: Using SET XACT_ABORT ON
Elements.BodyText: SET XACT_ABORT ON instructs SQL Server to automatically roll back the entire transaction when any run-time error occurs, simplifying straightforward procedures.
Elements.Notes: usp_ProcessOrderWithXactAbort and usp_BankTransfer both set XACT_ABORT ON at the top of the procedure.

Items.Text: With XACT_ABORT ON, simple procedures may not need a TRY...CATCH block at all.
It prevents the dangerous situation of a doomed transaction being left open after an error.
It pairs well with explicit transactions in financial procedures where partial completion is unacceptable.
Best practices recommend XACT_ABORT ON for simple cases and TRY...CATCH when custom handling or logging is required.

Elements.Title: Error Logging and Handling Specific Error Numbers
Elements.BodyText: Comprehensive error handling logs full diagnostic detail to a dedicated table and translates well-known SQL Server error numbers into meaningful messages.
Elements.Notes: An ErrorLog table typically stores ErrorTime, UserName, ErrorNumber, ErrorSeverity, ErrorState, ErrorProcedure, ErrorLine, and ErrorMessage.

Items.Text: Roll back first, then insert the log row so the logging INSERT itself is not undone.
Capture SUSER_SNAME() and ERROR_PROCEDURE() to identify who and what failed.
Error 2627 indicates a unique constraint violation — report 'Username or email already exists'.
Error 547 indicates a foreign key violation — report an invalid reference to a related table.
Error 1205 indicates a deadlock victim — implement retry logic rather than simply failing.
Fall through to THROW for any unrecognized error so nothing is silently swallowed.

Elements.Title: How Nested Transactions Really Behave
Elements.BodyText: SQL Server does not truly support nested transactions; additional BEGIN TRANSACTION statements only increment @@TRANCOUNT.
Elements.Notes: Example: BEGIN TRAN (@@TRANCOUNT=1), BEGIN TRAN (@@TRANCOUNT=2), COMMIT (@@TRANCOUNT=1, nothing committed), COMMIT (@@TRANCOUNT=0, everything commits).

Items.Text: Only the outermost COMMIT actually makes changes permanent.
A ROLLBACK at any nesting level rolls back the entire outer transaction.
Inner COMMIT statements merely decrement @@TRANCOUNT without persisting anything.
This behaviour surprises developers who expect independent inner transactions.
Never nest transactions without first checking @@TRANCOUNT.

Elements.Title: Safe Coordination Between Procedures Using @@TRANCOUNT and Savepoints
Elements.BodyText: Callable procedures should detect whether a transaction is already active and use a flag so that only the procedure that started a transaction commits or rolls it back.
Elements.Notes: usp_InnerProcedure sets @TranStarted = 1 only when @@TRANCOUNT = 0, and usp_OuterProcedure wraps multiple EXEC calls in a single transaction.

Items.Text: Declare a BIT flag such as @TranStarted and set it to 1 only if the procedure opened the transaction.
Commit only when @TranStarted = 1; otherwise let the caller decide.
In CATCH, roll back only if @TranStarted = 1 AND @@TRANCOUNT > 0, then THROW to propagate the error.
Use SAVE TRANSACTION SavePointName before risky steps and ROLLBACK TRANSACTION SavePointName to undo just that step.
Partial rollback lets you keep an order row while logging the failure and setting status to 'Pending Review'.
An outer procedure can coordinate several child procedures (create order, add items, shipping, payment, shipment) in one atomic unit.

Topics.Title: Distributed Transactions and the Saga Pattern
Topics.Summary: Explores cross-database and cross-server transactions using MS-DTC, BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION, and two-phase commit, along with their performance and availability challenges. Presents the Saga pattern with compensating transactions as a modern alternative for microservice architectures.

Elements.Title: What Distributed Transactions Are
Elements.BodyText: A distributed transaction is a logical unit of work that spans multiple databases, servers, or resource managers, requiring coordination so that all participants commit or roll back together.
Elements.Notes: Common scenarios include updating a local Orders table while simultaneously decrementing inventory in a remote warehouse database via a linked server.

Items.Text: Each participating system is a separate resource manager with its own transaction log.
ACID guarantees must be extended across machine and network boundaries.
A transaction coordinator is required to arbitrate the final commit or rollback decision.
Typical uses are cross-database operations within a server and cross-server operations over linked servers.

Elements.Title: Coordination Technologies: MS-DTC, 2PC, and Saga
Elements.BodyText: Three main technologies address distributed coordination, each suited to a different platform and style of system.

Items.Text: MS-DTC runs on Windows with SQL Server and coordinates cross-database and cross-server transactions.
Two-Phase Commit (2PC) is supported by most RDBMS platforms and underpins traditional distributed transactions.
The Saga pattern targets microservice architectures and long-running work using compensating transactions.
MS-DTC must be installed, configured, and enabled on every participating server before distributed transactions will work.

Elements.Title: BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION in T-SQL
Elements.BodyText: SQL Server exposes distributed transactions through the BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION statement, which enlists MS-DTC to coordinate the commit across all participants.
Elements.Notes: Example: BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION; UPDATE LocalDB.dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Completed' WHERE OrderID = 1; UPDATE RemoteServer.RemoteDB.dbo.Inventory SET Quantity = Quantity - 1 WHERE ProductID = 5; COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Items.Text: Statements inside the transaction can reference local objects and remote objects through linked servers.
A single COMMIT TRANSACTION tells MS-DTC to commit on every enlisted resource manager.
If any participant cannot commit, MS-DTC rolls back the work on all participants.
Four-part naming (Server.Database.Schema.Object) is used to reach remote tables.

Elements.Title: How Two-Phase Commit Works
Elements.BodyText: Two-phase commit is the protocol that makes an all-or-nothing outcome possible across independent systems.

Items.Text: Phase 1 (prepare): the coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit, and each one durably writes its changes and votes yes or no.
Phase 2 (commit): if all votes are yes, the coordinator instructs everyone to commit; a single no triggers a global rollback.
Participants hold their locks between the prepare and commit phases, extending lock duration.
If the coordinator fails after prepare, participants may be left 'in doubt' until it recovers.

Elements.Title: Challenges of Distributed Transactions
Elements.BodyText: Distributed transactions deliver strong guarantees but carry significant performance, availability, and operational costs.
Elements.Notes: The best practice list states: do not use distributed transactions unless they are genuinely required.

Items.Text: Performance is noticeably slower than local transactions because of coordination round-trips.
Every participant must be available, so overall availability is the product of each system's availability.
Network latency and failures increase the chance of timeouts and in-doubt transactions.
Locks are held across multiple systems for longer, raising blocking and deadlock risk.
Complexity grows with more points of failure and required MS-DTC configuration on every node.

Elements.Title: The Saga Pattern with Compensating Transactions
Elements.BodyText: A saga replaces one global transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating action that semantically undoes it if a later step fails.
Elements.Notes: Example flow: create order (local transaction) → reserve inventory → process payment → confirm order; on failure, refund payment, release inventory, and set order status to 'Cancelled'.

Items.Text: Each step commits immediately in its own system, so no locks are held across services.
Progress flags such as @InventoryReserved and @PaymentProcessed record which steps completed.
The CATCH block runs compensating procedures in reverse order of the steps that succeeded.
Compensation is a business-level undo (a refund), not a database rollback of committed data.
The system is eventually consistent rather than immediately consistent during the saga.

Elements.Title: Choosing Between 2PC and Saga
Elements.BodyText: Selecting an approach depends on how tightly coupled the systems are, how long the work runs, and how much scalability and fault tolerance matter.
Elements.Notes: The quick reference checklist recommends considering the Saga pattern over distributed transactions for cross-database operations.

Items.Text: Use MS-DTC/2PC for short, tightly coupled operations inside a controlled environment that demand immediate consistency.
Prefer sagas for microservices, external API calls, and long-running workflows where blocking is unacceptable.
Sagas scale better and tolerate partial outages because each service commits independently.
Sagas shift complexity to the application, which must design and test every compensating action.
Never place external API calls inside a distributed transaction — do that work outside and keep database transactions short.

Topics.Title: Real-World Use Cases, Performance, and Best Practices
Topics.Summary: Walks through practical transactional procedures for banking transfers, e-commerce orders, inventory adjustment, and user registration. Concludes with performance guidance on transaction duration, lock contention, batching, monitoring, and a do/don't best-practice checklist.

Elements.Title: Banking: Account Transfer Procedure
Elements.BodyText: Financial transfers are the classic transaction use case — money must never be created or destroyed. A transfer procedure locks the source account, validates funds, moves the money, and records an audit entry atomically.
Elements.Notes: Example: usp_BankTransfer uses SET XACT_ABORT ON, reads the source balance WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK), and raises 'Insufficient funds' before touching any balances.

Items.Text: Use UPDLOCK/ROWLOCK hints when reading the source balance to prevent other sessions from changing it mid-transaction.
Check for sufficient funds and ROLLBACK with a clear RAISERROR message before performing any update.
Debit the source account and credit the destination account inside the same explicit transaction.
Insert a row into a Transactions or TransactionLog table so every movement of money is auditable.
A pre-transaction logging procedure (e.g., LogTransactionAttempt) can record the attempt and return a TransactionID for later success flagging.

Elements.Title: E-Commerce: Order Processing
Elements.BodyText: An e-commerce checkout touches many tables at once — order header, line items, inventory, payment, and cart — so all of it belongs in one transaction.
Elements.Notes: Example: usp_ProcessEcommerceOrder wraps the entire checkout in BEGIN TRY / BEGIN TRANSACTION with a @@TRANCOUNT-guarded ROLLBACK and THROW in the CATCH block.

Items.Text: Create the order header first and capture the new key with SCOPE_IDENTITY() for use by dependent inserts.
Transfer cart items into OrderItems, then decrement StockQuantity and increment ReservedQuantity in a single set-based UPDATE.
Compare @@ROWCOUNT against the expected item count to detect out-of-stock products and raise an error.
Recalculate the order total, record a pending payment row, clear the cart, and set the status to 'Confirmed' before committing.
Any failure rolls back the whole checkout so stock is never reserved for an order that does not exist.

Elements.Title: Inventory Adjustment with an Audit Trail
Elements.BodyText: Stock adjustments must change the quantity and record who changed it and why, as a single unit of work.
Elements.Notes: Example: usp_AdjustInventory reads the current quantity WITH (UPDLOCK), validates the result, updates Products, and writes an InventoryAudit row.

Items.Text: Read the current StockQuantity with an update lock so concurrent adjustments cannot interleave.
Raise an error if the product does not exist or if the adjustment would produce a negative inventory balance.
Update the stock level and LastUpdated timestamp only after validation succeeds.
Write an audit record capturing old quantity, new quantity, adjustment amount, reason, user, and date.
Commit only when both the update and the audit entry succeed, keeping stock and audit history in sync.

Elements.Title: User Registration with Related Data
Elements.BodyText: Creating a user account also means creating a profile, default preferences, a role assignment, and an activity log entry — a partially created user is a broken user.
Elements.Notes: Example: usp_RegisterUser inserts into Users, UserProfiles, UserPreferences, UserRoles, and ActivityLog within one transaction.

Items.Text: Insert the Users row first and capture @UserID with SCOPE_IDENTITY() for all child inserts.
Create the profile, default preferences (notifications, theme, language), and assign the default 'User' role.
Add an ActivityLog entry recording the registration event before committing.
In the CATCH block, test ERROR_NUMBER() = 2627 to convert a unique constraint violation into a friendly 'Username or email already exists' message.
Other domains follow the same multi-table pattern: healthcare records, airline seat booking, payroll, logistics, and student enrollment.

Elements.Title: Transaction Duration and Lock Contention
Elements.BodyText: The longer a transaction runs, the longer it holds locks and the greater the risk of blocking and deadlocks. Duration is the single biggest performance lever in transaction design.
Elements.Notes: Guidance: under 1 second is ideal; 1–5 seconds is acceptable; 5–10 seconds signals a need to optimize; over 10 seconds requires redesign.

Items.Text: Do all validation and lookups before BEGIN TRANSACTION so locks are held for the minimum time.
Never include user interaction, WAITFOR delays, or external API calls inside a transaction — do that work outside and commit the result.
Access tables in a consistent order across all procedures to avoid circular lock waits and deadlocks.
Choose isolation levels to match the workload: READ UNCOMMITTED or SNAPSHOT for reporting, READ COMMITTED or SNAPSHOT for high-concurrency updates.

Elements.Title: Batching Large Operations and Monitoring
Elements.BodyText: Massive single-statement updates create huge transactions and long lock holds; splitting them into batches keeps the system responsive. Monitoring tells you when transactions are running too long.
Elements.Notes: Use sys.dm_tran_active_transactions joined to sys.dm_tran_session_transactions and sys.dm_exec_sessions to find long runners; DBCC SQLPERF(LOGSPACE) shows log usage.

Items.Text: Use a WHILE loop with UPDATE TOP (@BatchSize) and check @@ROWCOUNT to process archival or bulk changes incrementally.
Commit each batch separately and add a brief WAITFOR DELAY so other transactions can acquire locks.
Query the transaction DMVs filtered on DATEDIFF(SECOND, transaction_begin_time, GETDATE()) > 10 to surface long-running transactions.
Inspect sys.dm_tran_locks and sys.dm_exec_requests to identify blocking chains and wait times.
Monitor transaction log space regularly, since large uncommitted transactions prevent log truncation.

Elements.Title: Best-Practice Do and Don't Checklist
Elements.BodyText: A short checklist captures the habits that keep transactional code correct, fast, and maintainable.
Elements.Notes: Quick reference: single statements can rely on autocommit; multiple related operations need an explicit transaction with TRY...CATCH; cross-database work should favour the Saga pattern over distributed transactions.

Items.Text: Do keep transactions short, validate first, wrap work in TRY...CATCH, and check @@TRANCOUNT before ROLLBACK.
Do use XACT_ABORT ON for simple cases, log errors comprehensively, and test rollback paths deliberately.
Don't leave a transaction open after an error, hold locks longer than necessary, or use high isolation levels without need.
Don't nest transactions without checking @@TRANCOUNT, skip validation to save time, or assume a transaction will always succeed.
Document transaction expectations in each procedure header so callers know whether they must manage the transaction.
